newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia opposition tries to check rise of Chubais.
newsitem.headline: Russia opposition tries to check rise of Chubais.

text.p: Russia's opposition have turned their guns on Kremlin chief of staff Anatoly Chubais in an effort to check the rise of a man who has arguably become Russia's most influential politician.

While President Boris Yeltsin awaits heart surgery, Chubais has steadily been accumulating such power that critics say he is running the country rather than the Kremlin leader's constitutional deputy, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.

To his allies, Chubais is the man most responsible for steadying the boat in Yeltsin's absence, mapping out policy and plotting intrigues which culminated in the sacking of ambitious security adviser Alexander Lebed.
For opposition leaders of all hues but particularly the communists, the major opposition party, the young man with the ginger hair is a "bete noire" whom they have long sought to cut down to size.

They appear to believe the appointment on Tuesday of close Chubais ally Boris Berezovsky to Yeltsin's advisory Security Council, despite his lack of knowledge of security matters, provides the perfect ammunition for an offensive.
"There should be no regents like Chubais...We are saying do not turn executive power into a circus," Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov said.

Liberal leader Grigory Yavlinsky said: "The appointment of Berezovsky is scandalous incompetence by the presidential structures. I can only guess what other nominations Anatoly Chubais will make from now on."
Chubais has become the opposition's main target following the sacking of Lebed, who had been savaged in parliament over a controversial peace deal for rebel Chechnya.
Attacks on Chubais represent an attack on perhaps the most important pillar in the structures which the 65-year-old president has created to try to consolidate power.

Chubais, a 41-year-old economist, has long been despised by the communists, and many ordinary Russians, because of his role in privatisation and market reforms as a first deputy prime minister -- a post he lost last January.

But anger has mounted since he masterminded Yeltsin's election victory over Zyuganov on July 3 and was promptly promoted to head a streamlined presidential administration, combining the powers previously held by several officials.

"A covert political coup has taken place in Russia since the presidential election (last July)," Pavel Voshchanov, Yeltsin's former press secretary, wrote in the newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda on Thursday.
"All power is now concentrated in the hands of representatives of the clan headed by Anatoly Chubais."

Chubais' job description is loose and his role is clearly limited if the president is healthy. But while Yeltsin prepares for heart surgery, Chubais has had a big say in who has access to the president and taken on a much wider role.

The extent of his string-pulling behind the scenes is hard to gauge, as is the importance of his reported alliance with Yeltsin's daughter Tatyana Dyachenko, who is said to wield influence over her father.
Chubais has leading roles on a new commission hunting down tax-dodging companies, on the Security Council and on the recently formed advisory Defence Council.
"It is no secret that...85 percent of decisions are being taken by Chubais," Vyacheslav Igrunov, a liberal member of parliament.
He has also been appointed one of four men on a consultative council set up by Yeltsin this month to improve cooperation between government, parliament and the Kremlin.

Chubais' eventual aims are unclear. He has little chance of becoming president, or certainly not for some years. But he could be a powerful ally for Chernomyrdin, with whom he is widely said to have good relations, or to other centrist presidential hopefuls.
